reference.source: ASCRS Textbook of Colon and Rectal Surgery
clinicalPearls: Characterised by sudden, severe, cramping or stabbing pain in the anus or lower rectum lasting seconds to a few minutes, then resolving completely
Attacks are infrequent and often nocturnal, waking the patient from sleep, with no symptoms between episodes
Examination between attacks is normal, and it is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion
Distinguished from levator ani syndrome by the brevity of the episodes, seconds to minutes rather than twenty minutes or more
Thought to relate to transient spasm of the anal sphincter or pelvic floor smooth muscle
Because attacks are brief and self-limiting, treatment is largely reassurance; frequent severe episodes may respond to smooth-muscle relaxants, warm baths, or topical agents
A familial form associated with hereditary internal anal sphincter myopathy is recognised
reference.pathophysiology: Proctalgia fugax is a functional anorectal pain disorder attributed to paroxysmal spasm of the smooth muscle of the anal canal or pelvic floor, sometimes involving the internal anal sphincter. Attacks are brief and self-limiting with no structural correlate. Triggers include stress, sexual activity, and defecation, and a rare hereditary internal anal sphincter myopathy underlies some familial cases. Between episodes there is no demonstrable abnormality.
additionalInvestigations: History to confirm brief, self-limiting attacks with symptom-free intervals
Digital rectal examination and proctoscopy between attacks to exclude local pathology
Anorectal manometry in atypical or frequent cases
Endoanal ultrasound if hereditary internal sphincter myopathy is suspected (thickened internal sphincter)
Sigmoidoscopy or colonoscopy where alarm features warrant exclusion of other disease
Pelvic imaging where a structural or neurological cause is suspected
redFlags: Rectal bleeding, weight loss, or a mass suggesting organic disease
Persistent rather than fleeting pain, pointing to another diagnosis
Progressive or nocturnal pain with neurological features
Onset in later life without any prior episodes
reference.prognosis: A benign condition; although attacks can be intensely painful, they are brief, self-limiting, and cause no lasting harm, with many patients experiencing only occasional episodes.
pitfalls: Confusing the brief attacks with the sustained ache of levator ani syndrome
Missing an anal fissure or thrombosed haemorrhoid as the true cause
Overlooking the rare hereditary internal anal sphincter myopathy in familial cases
